posts.caption: The photographer arrived at three with a ring light and a lot of confidence. I'd spent forty minutes that morning braiding, so I stood at the stall door and watched him shoot forty frames of a horse who had decided to be the best-looking thing in the county. He kept adjusting the light. She kept adjusting her chin. At one point the barn cat walked through the frame and got more usable shots than I did. The proofs came back Friday. Every one of them looked exactly like her, and I paid for all of them.
posts.first: I once spent an entire Saturday detangling a forelock for a photo that got cropped to just her ears. She posed for it like it was the cover of something. We hung it on the tack room wall anyway. It's the best picture in there.

posts.caption: My sister-in-law visited the barn for the first time on Sunday. She wore white sneakers, which I decided not to mention. I gave her the full tour: the tack room, the feed room, the wash rack, the good hay and the bad hay. She asked a lot of kind, reasonable questions that no horse person has ever needed answered. Big Red watched all of it from the wash rack with her hoof up, like a security guard. When we got to the gate my sister-in-law said it was all very peaceful. Then she looked down. The sneakers were brown.
posts.first: Twenty years ago my father asked why I was so cold at the barn all winter, then wore two coats to my first show. We've never discussed it. He still sits in the truck with the heater running and calls it supervising.

posts.caption: Her mother started riding him at nine, back when he was young enough to bolt at a plastic bag. Now she's thirty-eight and she brought the next one. The little girl is four and fearless and keeps calling him 'Mister Horse.' I held the lead rope and tried to look like I wasn't crying. He stood so still a sparrow landed on his saddle pad. Her mother got out her phone and stopped halfway. She just watched instead. It took them about eleven minutes to finish one lap of the arena.
posts.first: He taught me how to sit a trot in 2006 by simply refusing to go faster than I could manage. I've never found a better teacher. He's twenty-eight now, and I still apologize when I mount him, even though he doesn't need it.

posts.quote: My farrier hasn't raised his price in two years. I now ask about his knees the way other people check the stock market.
posts.first: My farrier's back went out two winters ago and he worked the whole week bent sideways. I brought him a heating pad and a thermos, and he took both without comment. Since then I schedule him on the days I can bring soup. He doesn't ask. I don't mention it.

posts.caption: The hay delivery came at 7:15, which is the exact hour the barn is least organized. I opened the trailer ramp to start stacking. Pudding walked straight past me, climbed in, and stood in the middle like a statue. I tried treats. I tried the lead rope. I tried reasoning with him, which has never worked once. Eventually I unloaded all one hundred and twenty bales around him while he supervised with his chin up. The hay guy took a photo for his wife. He did not offer to help.
posts.first: My first pony did the exact same thing with a pickup truck bed in 1994. I stood in the yard for an hour while my dad pretended this was normal. Eventually he drove the truck around the block, pony and all. The pony got off at the barn like he'd planned it.

posts.caption: The forecast said sleet starting at noon, and by 12:05 the whole barn had gone quiet in that way it only does in bad weather. I brought the mash out early and sat on an upturned bucket outside her stall. The roof sounded like somebody emptying a bag of gravel. She ate slowly, one ear turned toward the door, never in a hurry. I had a list of things to do. I didn't do any of them. Around three I realized I'd been sitting there for two hours. The sleet was still going. So was I.
posts.first: My mother used to say the best weather for a barn is the kind you don't have to drive in. I laughed at her for years. Now I drive home slowly in the dark with the heater on, and I know exactly what she meant.
